interop.title: Interoperability and data exchange
interop.subtitle: Exchanging SNOMED CT-coded data between systems, with examples in HL7 FHIR
interop.overview: Interoperability depends on systems agreeing not only on how data is structured, but on what it means. SNOMED CT provides that shared meaning: a single, precise identifier for each clinical idea - a diagnosis, finding, procedure, substance, or allergy - independent of the language, display term, or system in which it was recorded. Because every concept sits within a hierarchy and a formal concept model, a receiving system can do more than display the data: - Validate it against agreed value sets - Aggregate it by subsumption - Present it in the user's language - Use it directly in decision support and analytics Realising this requires sender and receiver to agree on which concepts are valid for each data element, how coded data is validated, and how terms are displayed. SNOMED CT is independent of any particular exchange standard and is used with HL7 CDA, HL7 v2, openEHR, IHE profiles, and others. HL7 FHIR is today the most widely adopted standard for health data exchange, so this playbook uses it for its examples. In FHIR: - Resources such as Condition, Observation, Procedure, and AllergyIntolerance carry SNOMED CT codes - Terminology bindings define which value sets - typically expressed as ECL constraints - are valid for each coded element - A FHIR Terminology Service, implementing operations such as $expand, $validate-code, $lookup, $subsumes, and $translate, validates, expands, and translates SNOMED CT content at runtime The same principles apply to other exchange standards. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment guidance.

decisions.question: Which data elements will carry SNOMED CT codes, and how strictly will each binding be enforced?
decisions.guidance: Identify each coded element in your exchange, where it sits in the exchange structure, and how strictly its value set is enforced. In FHIR, this is the resource and element path and the binding strength: required bindings enforce conformance, while extensible and preferred bindings allow alternatives. Binding strictness has significant implications for receiver systems - a strict binding means validation failures block processing, while looser bindings allow locally-defined alternatives.

decisions.question: Which SNOMED CT edition and version will be declared in exchanged data?
decisions.guidance: Senders must declare the code system and, where precision matters, the SNOMED CT edition and version. In FHIR, this is the system URI (http://snomed.info/sct) and the version URI (e.g., http://snomed.info/sct/32506021000036107 for the Australian edition); other standards carry the same information in their own code system and version fields. Receivers need this to validate codes correctly. Agree version declaration policy with all exchange partners before go-live.

decisions.question: How will receiving systems validate incoming SNOMED CT codes?
decisions.guidance: Receivers should validate incoming concept IDs against their terminology service (in FHIR, with the $validate-code operation) to confirm that they are active, valid for the declared SNOMED CT edition/version, and within the expected value set. Accepting codes without validation allows invalid or out-of-scope data into clinical systems.

decisions.question: What display text strategy will be used for different locales?
decisions.guidance: The display text shown to users must be the preferred term from the receiver's language reference set - not the sender's preferred term, not the FSN. Retrieve it from the terminology service using the target language reference set (in FHIR, with the $lookup operation). Coordinate display text handling with exchange partners, particularly in multilingual or cross-national exchanges.

decisions.question: How will SNOMED CT releases be coordinated across exchange partners?
decisions.guidance: When a sender updates to a new SNOMED CT release before receivers do, concept IDs may temporarily be unresolvable on receiver systems. Agree a release coordination policy - including a transition window - with all exchange partners before upgrading. Ensure all stakeholders have access to the version of SNOMED CT declared in exchanged messages, or have access to a terminology server that holds the required versions, such as one hosted by the national release centre or a multi-edition server, to resolve version mismatches.

decisions.question: What is the resolution strategy when a received concept cannot be validated due to a version or edition mismatch?
decisions.guidance: Two failure modes require different resolution strategies. (1) Concept not found: the sender may be using a newer release or a different national edition - in both cases validation returns 'not found'. Check the national terminology server first for a newer version of the national edition; if still unresolved, query a multi-edition server for the closest international ancestor. (2) Concept inactive: the sender used an older release - apply the proposed replacement from SNOMED CT's historical association reference sets. Define and document these strategies for each exchange partner relationship before go-live.

steps.title: Map each exchanged data element to its structure and terminology binding
steps.description: Create a data mapping document that identifies every SNOMED CT-coded element in the exchange, where it sits in the exchange structure, the value set that constrains it (expressed as an ECL constraint or reference set), and how strictly that binding is enforced. In FHIR, this means the resource and element path (e.g., Condition.code) and the binding strength (required, extensible, preferred); other standards express the same information through their own structures, such as CDA templates or openEHR archetype nodes. If the exchange is governed by a formal, computable implementation guide - such as a FHIR Implementation Guide, whose profiles declare the element paths, value set bindings, and binding strengths, or the equivalent CDA templates or openEHR templates - most of this mapping is already defined and should be reused rather than recreated. What remains is mapping your own system's data to those profiles, and checking that the guide's value sets use SNOMED CT with an appropriate ECL constraint and a declared edition and version. See the Value set playbook for guidance on defining ECL-based value sets. The Terminology Bindings Sandbox lets you try out bindings interactively.

examples.label: FHIR Condition with SNOMED CT coding

steps.title: Define a value set for each terminology binding using ECL
steps.description: Write an ECL expression for each coded element (e.g., <<404684003 |Clinical finding| for a condition or problem code). Publish each value set with a stable identifier and an explicit SNOMED CT edition and version, so that sender and receiver validate against the same content. In FHIR, value sets are packaged as ValueSet resources with canonical URLs, with the edition and version declared in the compose. See the Value set playbook for ECL authoring and packaging guidance.

examples.label: FHIR ValueSet with ECL binding (intensional)

steps.title: Deploy or configure a terminology service
steps.description: Ensure a terminology service is available to both sender and receiver systems. It must support the SNOMED CT services that exchange relies on: expanding value sets from ECL, validating codes, looking up terms and properties, testing subsumption, and translating through maps (see the Mapping playbook). The FHIR Terminology Service API is the most widely implemented interface for these services ($expand, $validate-code, $lookup, $subsumes, $translate), and a FHIR R4-compliant server can support exchanges built on other standards as well. Implementers must deploy or license their own terminology service for production use - the public terminology server operated by SNOMED International is intended for evaluation and testing only, not for production clinical systems. See the Terminology service playbook for full deployment guidance.

options.label: SELF-HOSTED TERMINOLOGY SERVICE
points: Deploy Snowstorm (open source, FHIR R4-compliant) on your own infrastructure
Load the required SNOMED CT edition(s) from licensed RF2 release files
Full control over editions, versions, and language reference set configuration
Requires infrastructure capacity and an operational release upgrade process
Recommended for production clinical systems with high availability requirements

example.label: Snowstorm FHIR base URL
example.code:
# Snowstorm FHIR R4 endpoint (self-hosted)
Base URL: https://your-snowstorm-server/fhir

# Test the server is running
GET https://your-snowstorm-server/fhir/metadata

# List loaded code systems
GET https://your-snowstorm-server/fhir/CodeSystem?system=http://snomed.info/sct

options.label: PUBLIC OR HOSTED TERMINOLOGY SERVICE
points: The public SNOMED International terminology server is for evaluation and testing only - not for production use by implementers
For production, use a terminology service hosted by your national release centre (NRC) or a licensed commercial provider
Reduces operational burden - no infrastructure to provision or upgrade pipeline to manage
Multi-edition servers can resolve concepts from editions not available locally
Assess latency, uptime SLA, and data sovereignty requirements before selecting a hosted provider

steps.title: Validate coded data on receipt
steps.description: When data is received, validate each SNOMED CT-coded element against the declared edition/version and the expected value set (in FHIR, with the $validate-code operation). If validation succeeds, the concept is active and within scope - proceed normally. If validation fails, identify the failure mode and apply the corresponding resolution strategy. In all cases, preserve both the original received code and the locally resolved code in the record so the substitution is auditable. Define and document these strategies for each exchange partner relationship before go-live.

options.label: CONCEPT NOT FOUND
points: The sender may be using a newer release or a different national edition
Check the national terminology server first for a newer version of the national edition
If still unresolved, query a multi-edition server for the closest international ancestor
Log unresolved cases for review with the exchange partner

options.label: CONCEPT INACTIVE
points: The sender used an older release in which the concept was still active
Apply the proposed replacement from SNOMED CT's historical association reference sets
Historical association types: SAME AS, REPLACED BY, POSSIBLY EQUIVALENT TO - use in order of confidence
Where no unambiguous replacement exists, flag for clinical review before processing

examples.label: $validate-code - success response
examples.code:
# Validate a concept against a value set
GET /fhir/ValueSet/$validate-code
  ?url=https://example.org/ValueSet/condition-code-value-set
  &system=http://snomed.info/sct
  &systemVersion=http://snomed.info/sct/900000000000207008/version/20250301
  &code=44054006

# Success response
{
  "resourceType": "Parameters",
  "parameter": [
    { "name": "result", "valueBoolean": true },
    { "name": "display", "valueString": "Diabetes mellitus type 2" },
    { "name": "version", "valueString": "http://snomed.info/sct/900000000000207008/version/20250301" }
  ]
}

examples.label: $validate-code - failure responses

steps.title: Display received concepts using the receiver's language reference set
steps.description: When rendering received SNOMED CT codes, retrieve the preferred term from the receiver's language reference set through the terminology service (in FHIR, $lookup with the displayLanguage parameter). Display the resulting preferred term - do not treat the display text in the received data as authoritative, as it reflects the sender's locale. Good practice is to preserve the sender's original display text as a secondary label or tooltip so clinicians can see what the sending system recorded - this matters when preferred terms differ significantly across locales for the same concept. When a concept has been resolved via a mismatch strategy, indicate the original received concept to the user if clinically relevant.

examples.label: $lookup with language reference set parameter

steps.title: Test end-to-end with conformance tooling
steps.description: Validate exchanges with the conformance tooling of the exchange standard in use and, where applicable, IHE or HL7 connectathon test scripts. Confirm that coded data round-trips correctly - codes sent are correctly validated and displayed at the receiver. Specifically test version and edition mismatch scenarios: send concepts from a newer version and from an older version, and verify the resolution strategies produce the expected outcomes. For FHIR, use the FHIR Validator (validator.fhir.org) to confirm resource conformance against published profiles.

dependencies.text: FHIR R4-compliant terminology service ($expand, $validate-code, $lookup, $subsumes, $translate)
FHIR R4 server or integration layer at sender and receiver
Language reference sets configured for each locale involved in exchange
SNOMED CT license for all participating organisations

pitfalls: Sending the FSN as the display text - receivers will display a technical label to clinicians rather than the appropriate preferred term
Not declaring the SNOMED CT edition and version in exchanged data - receivers cannot validate codes without knowing which edition and version was used
Accepting incoming codes without validation - invalid or retired concept IDs silently enter clinical systems

Treating all validation failures as equivalent, or having no resolution strategy for them - a concept from a newer version, an inactivated concept, and a concept from a different edition each require a different resolution; logging and escalating is not sufficient - receivers must be able to resolve concepts from newer or older versions using a terminology server that holds the required versions and SNOMED CT history supplements

Using extension concepts not available in receiver systems without providing the nearest international ancestor - receivers in a different edition cannot resolve or validate locally created extension concepts
No release coordination policy across exchange partners - a SNOMED CT upgrade on one side causes validation failures on the other without an agreed resolution pathway
Recreating bindings that a formal implementation guide already defines - local re-mapping diverges from the guide and from other implementers
Treating the display text in received data as authoritative - it reflects the sender's language and locale, not the receiver's

value-sets.title: Value set design and management
value-sets.subtitle: Designing, authoring, and maintaining SNOMED CT value sets using ECL and reference sets
value-sets.overview: A value set is a uniquely identifiable set of valid concept identifiers selected from one or more code systems for use in a specific context. When using SNOMED CT, value sets define which concepts are valid for a given data element such as a problem list, a diagnosis field, or a procedure picker. A value set can be defined in three ways: - Intensionally (recommended), using Expression Constraint Language (ECL): an expression that captures the intended concept scope from the SNOMED CT hierarchy. ECL-based definitions improve maintenance: new concepts that satisfy the constraint are included automatically when the ECL is executed against a new release, and a terminology service can evaluate them at runtime against the chosen SNOMED CT edition and version. - Extensionally, as an explicit list of concepts, where the intended scope is a curated selection that ECL cannot express, or where a fixed list is required. Extensional definitions do not pick up new concepts, so each SNOMED CT release needs a review both to replace inactivated members and to identify new concepts that should be added. - Mix of both: intensional and extensional approaches can be combined, with an ECL rule plus explicitly included or excluded concepts. A SNOMED CT subset is a closely related idea: a set of SNOMED CT components (usually concepts) selected for a purpose, built by query, by manual selection, or by a combination of both. Unlike a value set, a subset contains only SNOMED CT content and is shared as an explicit list of members - sometimes as an RF2 reference set, though many implementers use other formats. A value set can span several code systems and can be defined by a rule that is executed when needed, so a subset corresponds to a value set's expansion rather than its definition.

decisions.question: What is the clinical purpose and context of this value set?
decisions.guidance: Before defining any constraints, document exactly what the value set is for (for example a picklist, decision support rule, analytics cohort, or messaging constraint), what must be in or out, and the consequences of including or excluding borderline concepts. Identify where it will be used: the information model element it binds to, the binding strength (for example, FHIR’s required, extensible, preferred, or example binding strengths), and the people or systems that consume it. This specification is the basis for all subsequent design decisions and is required before governance sign-off.

decisions.question: Should the value set be defined by query (ECL), manual list, or a hybrid?
decisions.guidance: Query-based (intensional) ECL definitions are strongly preferred when members follow a logical pattern, such as << 73211009 |Diabetes mellitus|. They are largely self-maintaining, because executing the ECL against a new release picks up new members, though each release should still be checked for unintended changes caused by remodelling or inactivation. A manual (extensional) list is appropriate when there is no consistent pattern, such as a small, locally prioritised shortlist where clinical judgement over individual concepts is required, or when a fixed list is needed. It gives precise control but takes more effort, and it drifts out of date because new concepts are never added automatically. A hybrid approach is often practical: generate the core set with a query, then add or remove a few concepts explicitly, reviewing those explicit changes on each release.

decisions.question: What SNOMED CT hierarchy, attribute constraint, or reference set membership best captures the clinical scope?
decisions.guidance: Explore the SNOMED CT Browser to find the most specific ancestor concept, or concepts, that cover the intended content, using exclusions where an ancestor brings in unwanted descendants. Consider whether attribute refinement (e.g. finding site, causative agent) is needed for precision, and check the expansion for relevant concepts that are missed because they lack the defining attribute. Reference set membership can also be used as a constraint, either on its own or combined with a hierarchy (e.g. restricting a hierarchy to members of an existing reference set). Finally, check whether an existing reference set or FHIR ValueSet already covers your need before authoring a new one.

decisions.question: What does the value set depend on, and what depends on it?
decisions.guidance: Record the SNOMED CT edition and version it is built against, any reference sets, other code systems or value sets it draws on, whether it is pinned to a specific version or expanded against the latest release, and the terminology services or systems that will expand it. List the downstream consumers (forms, rules, reports, interfaces) and their owners that will be affected when it changes, so impact can be assessed on every SNOMED CT release and whenever the value set or its dependencies change.

decisions.question: How will the value set be delivered to and consumed by clinical systems?
decisions.guidance: Integrating a FHIR terminology service is best practice: it enables live ECL expansion, preferred term retrieval, and concept search at runtime. Where direct integration is not feasible, the value set must be exported as a static representation (FHIR ValueSet with explicit entries, CSV, or RF2 reference set) and refreshed on each SNOMED CT release. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment options.

decisions.question: How should the value set be packaged and distributed?
decisions.guidance: RF2 simple type reference sets are the native SNOMED CT format and are supported by terminology servers and RF2-aware authoring tools. FHIR ValueSet resources are required for FHIR-based systems and support ECL via compose.include.filter. A simple list (a spreadsheet or text file of SCTIDs with terms) can suit reviewers and systems with no terminology integration, but it is a snapshot that must be regenerated on each release. Agree the format with consuming systems before authoring.

decisions.question: Who has clinical authority to approve content, and what is the review cadence?
decisions.guidance: Every value set requires a named clinical owner who approves the initial content and reviews it on each SNOMED CT release. Define the governance process, approval workflow, and minimum review frequency before the value set is used in production.

steps.title: Define the clinical purpose and scope
steps.description: Document exactly what the value set is for, who will use it, in what clinical context, and what the consequences of including or excluding borderline concepts are. This clinical specification is the basis for all subsequent design decisions and must be agreed with clinical and governance leads before authoring begins.

steps.title: Explore the SNOMED CT hierarchy and define the concept scope
steps.description: Navigate the SNOMED CT hierarchy using an available browser or authoring tool to identify the most appropriate ancestor concept or concepts, any necessary attribute refinements, and any exclusions needed to remove unwanted descendants. Reference set membership can also be used as a constraint. Review whether existing reference sets or value sets already meet your need before creating a new one. Choose a definition approach based on whether clinical intent can be expressed as an ECL expression.

options.label: INTENSIONAL DEFINITION
points: Write an ECL expression (e.g. << 73211009 |Diabetes mellitus|) that captures the intended scope
A terminology server expands it when requested, against the chosen SNOMED CT edition and version
New subtypes in future releases are included automatically
Preferred approach: requires less maintenance, but each release should still be checked for unintended changes caused by remodelling or inactivation

options.label: EXTENSIONAL DEFINITION
points: Manually select individual concepts where the scope cannot be expressed as a hierarchy or attribute pattern, such as a locally prioritised shortlist, or where a fixed list is required
Gives precise control over membership
New concepts are never added automatically, so each release needs a review to replace inactivated members and identify new concepts to add

options.label: HYBRID
points: Generate the core set with ECL, then explicitly add or remove a small number of concepts
Review the explicit additions and removals on each release

steps.title: Build, test, and clinically review
steps.description: Write an ECL expression using subsumption (<<), attribute refinements, and set operators as needed, then expand it using the Browser's ECL search or the FHIR $expand endpoint. Check the expansion for unexpected inclusions and omissions. For manual or hybrid sets, confirm that every explicitly listed concept is active in the target release. Have clinical SMEs review the expanded concept list, not just the ECL, even when the query looks right, and record who approved it and why.

examples.label: ECL expression
examples.code:
# All clinical findings (broad scope)
<<404684003 |Clinical finding (finding)|

# Descendants and self: diabetes mellitus
<<73211009 |Diabetes mellitus|

# Narrowed to disorders only
<<64572001 |Disease (disorder)|

# Attribute refinement: findings with finding site = heart structure
<<404684003 |Clinical finding| : 363698007 |Finding site| = <<80891009 |Heart structure|

# Exclusion: diabetes mellitus, excluding diabetes in pregnancy
<<73211009 |Diabetes mellitus| MINUS <<199223000 |Maternal diabetes mellitus during antenatal and/or intrapartum and/or postpartum period|

# Refset membership: restrict a hierarchy to members of a reference set
<<64572001 |Disease (disorder)| AND ^ [refset id] |[refset name]|

examples.label: FHIR $expand call
examples.code:
GET /fhir/ValueSet/$expand?url=http://snomed.info/sct?fhir_vs=ecl/<<404684003&count=10

# With edition and display language
GET /fhir/ValueSet/$expand
  ?url=http://snomed.info/sct?fhir_vs=ecl/<<404684003
  &system-version=http://snomed.info/sct|http://snomed.info/sct/900000000000207008/version/20261101
  &displayLanguage=en
  &count=20
  &offset=0

steps.title: Choose how the value set will be delivered
steps.description: Integrating a FHIR terminology service directly into the clinical system is best practice: it enables live ECL expansion, concept search, and preferred term retrieval against the chosen SNOMED CT edition and version. Where direct integration is not feasible, a separate terminology server can be used to expand the value set and export it. An exported list must include preferred terms and be packaged in a structured format, because a raw list of concept IDs is not a usable value set, and it must be refreshed on each SNOMED CT release. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment and integration guidance.

steps.title: Represent the value set in a form the clinical system can use
steps.description: A list of concept IDs alone is not sufficient: the clinical system needs terms and a structured format it can process. The right approach depends on your architecture.

options.label: FHIR terminology server integrated
points: Define a named FHIR ValueSet resource with an ECL expression in the compose element
The terminology server resolves preferred terms at runtime from the configured language reference set
No static export needed - the value set stays current with the chosen SNOMED CT edition and version

options.label: No integrated terminology server
points: Export the expanded concept list from a terminology server, including preferred and acceptable terms for your language

Package as a FHIR ValueSet with explicit concept entries, a CSV, or an RF2 reference set (typically a simple reference set). An RF2 reference set references components by ID and does not contain terms, so the system also needs the corresponding description and language reference set files to obtain them
Must be refreshed on each SNOMED CT release to pick up new or inactivated concepts

example.label: FHIR ValueSet with explicit entries (extensional)

steps.title: Author and publish with versioning
steps.description: Choose an authoring tool suited to the value set's complexity. For straightforward value sets and reference sets, lightweight tooling (such as Simplex, a free tool from SNOMED International) provides a streamlined workflow. For reference sets that need to be released as part of a SNOMED CT edition, a full authoring platform (such as the SNOMED Authoring Platform, available to national release centres and members) supports classification and validation. Commercial authoring tools are also available. Assign a canonical URI (for FHIR ValueSet) or a SCTID (for RF2 reference sets). Publish with version metadata aligned to the SNOMED CT release cycle, and define a change notification process for all consuming systems.

steps.title: Establish governance and release management
steps.description: Review the value set against each relevant SNOMED CT release, or at an agreed cadence that suits your edition’s release schedule: the International Edition is released monthly, and national extensions follow their own release cycles. Compare the new expansion with the previous one to confirm that added and removed concepts are intended, check that concepts referenced in the ECL or listed explicitly are still active, and identify new concepts that should be added to any explicit list. Define who reviews the value set, how records coded with inactivated concepts are handled (for example, by using historical associations in queries), and how consumers are notified of changes. Keep each definition and its change history in a versioned store, such as your terminology or authoring tool, or version control alongside implementation code. Agree a route for urgent changes between scheduled reviews. Test changes against the systems that use the value set in a staging environment, and notify them before the change goes live. See the Governance playbook for release management process guidance.

steps.title: Document the value set
steps.description: Capture the purpose and rationale, selection criteria (ECL and any manual additions or removals), the information model element and binding strength, dependencies, the SNOMED CT edition and version, the clinical review outcome and approver, the owner, and the review schedule. This record lets others reuse, audit, and maintain the value set without reverse-engineering it.

dependencies.text: Terminology service (integrated or standalone) with ECL expansion ($expand) support
Named clinical SMEs for scope definition and validation
Governance process for approval, versioning, and change notification

pitfalls: Using extensional (explicit list) definitions where ECL would suffice: lists require manual maintenance on every SNOMED CT release
Using a static value set extracted from a terminology server without a refresh process: new clinically relevant concepts added in SNOMED CT releases are silently excluded
No clinical review: value sets not validated by clinical SMEs may exclude concepts clinicians expect, or include concepts that are inappropriate in context
Publishing without versioning: consuming systems cannot detect changes and continue using stale pre-expanded sets
Not checking whether an existing value set meets the need: duplicating content that is already maintained creates unnecessary ongoing maintenance burden
No governance: value sets with no named clinical owner degrade in quality as the SNOMED CT release evolves
Clinical review of the ECL only: reviewers should see the expanded concept list, because a correct-looking query can still include or miss concepts in practice
Manual lists not checked for inactive concepts: an explicitly listed concept can be inactivated in a new release and silently break the value set
Ad hoc changes between reviews without notification: downstream queries, CDS rules, and cohort definitions break silently

term-service.title: Terminology service implementation
term-service.subtitle: Providing SNOMED CT terminology services to clinical applications, from use cases to deployment and version upgrades
term-service.overview: A SNOMED CT terminology service is the software function that gives applications access to SNOMED CT content: finding concepts, retrieving terms in the right language, testing subtypes and reference set membership, applying expression constraints, and identifying changes between versions. SNOMED CT delivers its full value only when these services use its specific features (the hierarchy, concept definitions, reference sets, expression constraints, language reference sets, and history), not just generic code lookup. A shared, SNOMED CT-enabled terminology server with an HL7 FHIR interface is the recommended approach; some systems instead implement selected services directly from the release files.

decisions.question: Which use cases must the terminology service support?
decisions.guidance: Start from what the consuming applications need to do, then derive the service types. The SNOMED CT Terminology Services Guide maps use cases to service types: data entry needs concept search, terms, subtype testing, reference set membership, and expression constraints; display needs terms for a concept; reporting and analytics need subsumption, reference set membership, and expression constraints; managing upgrades needs change identification and history data; and mapping needs map data. List the use cases for each consuming system before choosing or configuring a server.

decisions.question: Should services come from a shared terminology server or be built into each application?
decisions.guidance: A shared SNOMED CT-enabled terminology server is recommended: every application gets the same content, the same terms, and a single upgrade path. It can be self-hosted or provided by your National Release Centre (NRC) or a commercial provider. Applications can also implement selected services directly from the release files, which can suit simple needs such as display, but each application then carries its own upgrade and consistency burden. Public servers are for development and evaluation, not production clinical use.

decisions.question: Which editions, versions, and language reference sets are required?
decisions.guidance: Most implementations need their national edition, which combines the International Edition with national content such as local concepts, reference sets, and language reference sets. Agree which edition and version each consuming system uses, and make every service request identify them explicitly, because results differ between versions. Decide the language reference sets and their fallback order for each user group. See the Multilingual implementation playbook for language configuration.

decisions.question: Which interfaces will consuming systems use?
decisions.guidance: The HL7 FHIR terminology operations ($lookup, $expand, $validate-code, $subsumes, $translate) are the standard interface for clinical applications and support SNOMED CT through implicit value sets and ECL. Some SNOMED CT features, such as history data, change identification, concept model rules, and reference set data, may need the server's native API. Document which operations each consuming system calls and what it does when the service is unavailable. See the Interoperability playbook for FHIR exchange patterns.

decisions.question: How will you adopt new SNOMED CT versions?
decisions.guidance: The International Edition is released monthly, and national editions and derivatives follow their own cycles. Agree an upgrade cadence, then for each upgrade identify additions, changes, and inactivations, and use the historical association reference sets to find replacements for inactive content used in templates, value sets, and queries. If you skip versions, a single set of delta files will not cover all changes, so load from snapshot or full files. See the Governance playbook for change management.

decisions.question: What operational, performance, and licensing requirements apply?
decisions.guidance: Clinical applications that rely on the service for search and validation need high availability. Define service levels, access control, audit logging, and capacity before go-live. Design for statelessness and paging so the service scales, and agree where caching is acceptable and how caches are refreshed after upgrades. Make sure only licensed users and systems receive SNOMED CT content.

steps.title: Identify use cases and required service types
steps.description: For each consuming application, list the use cases it supports (for example data entry, display, reporting, mapping, or change management) and the service types each one needs. Use the use-case table in the Terminology Services Guide as a checklist. This list becomes the requirements for selecting, configuring, and testing the terminology service.

steps.title: Choose the deployment model
steps.description: Decide how the required services will be provided. A shared terminology server is the recommended approach for clinical applications; choose between self-hosting and a hosted service based on control, availability, data sovereignty, and operational capacity. Building services into an application from the release files is possible for limited needs, but plan for its upgrade and consistency burden.

options.label: SHARED TERMINOLOGY SERVER
points: Self-host a SNOMED CT-enabled terminology server (open source or commercial) or use one hosted by your NRC or a commercial provider
Gives every application the same content, the same terms, and a single upgrade path
Supports the full set of service types, including expression constraints, subsumption, and history
Use public servers for development and evaluation only, not for production clinical applications

options.label: SERVICES BUILT INTO THE APPLICATION
points: Preferred approach: use a separate terminology service to author and publish the required terminology artifacts (value sets, concept lists, preferred terms) as pre-created resources, then load them into the application's terminology storage
Loading RF2 release files directly into the application's storage is also a valid option, provided the application implements the required service types in compliance with the SNOMED CT specification
A relational database built from the release files is not a terminology server by itself: search, subsumption, and ECL expression constraints still need to be implemented correctly
Each application carries its own upgrade burden and must stay consistent with other systems when release files change

steps.title: Load the editions and versions you need
steps.description: Obtain licensed release packages from SNOMED International (via MLDS) or your NRC, and load the edition each consuming system needs, typically your national edition. Load from snapshot or full files for a first load or when versions have been skipped. Check content integrity and concept counts after loading, and make sure each edition and version can be selected explicitly in service requests.

options.label: NATIONAL EDITION
points: Combines the International Edition with national concepts, descriptions, and reference sets
Includes the national language reference set that clinicians need
Check with your NRC for the release schedule and how the edition is packaged

options.label: INTERNATIONAL EDITION ONLY
points: Appropriate when no national edition exists for your territory
Released monthly by SNOMED International
Add an international or local language reference set for display terms, and confirm that missing national content is acceptable

steps.title: Configure languages and terms
steps.description: Configure the language reference sets and fallback order for each user group so that search returns preferred terms and acceptable synonyms, and display returns the preferred term in the user's language. Every request that returns terms should state the language or language reference set. Test that fully specified names are never returned as display terms. See the Search and data entry playbook for how this affects clinician-facing search.

steps.title: Expose and test the service interfaces
steps.description: Enable the interfaces your consuming systems use, typically the HL7 FHIR terminology operations, plus native API calls for features FHIR does not cover. Test each required service type with realistic content: expansion with ECL, validation of valid, invalid, and inactive codes, subsumption, term lookup in each language, and map translation where needed. Confirm that every request identifies the edition and version.

examples.label: $expand with ECL
$validate-code
$subsumes
examples.code:
# Test whether Clinical finding (404684003) subsumes Diabetes mellitus (73211009)
GET /fhir/CodeSystem/$subsumes
  ?system=http://snomed.info/sct
  &codeA=404684003
  &codeB=73211009

# Response - codeA subsumes codeB (73211009 is a descendant of 404684003)
{
  "resourceType": "Parameters",
  "parameter": [
    { "name": "outcome", "valueCode": "subsumes" }
  ]
}

# Possible outcome values:
# "equivalent"  - codeA and codeB are the same concept
# "subsumes"    - codeA is an ancestor of codeB
# "subsumed-by" - codeA is a descendant of codeB
# "not-subsumed" - no subsumption relationship exists

steps.title: Integrate with consuming applications
steps.description: For each consuming system, document the service endpoint, the operations it calls, the edition and version, the value sets or ECL constraints per field, and the language configuration. Agree behaviour when the service is unavailable, and where caching is used, how caches are refreshed after an upgrade. See the Value set design and management playbook for how consuming systems define and reference value sets.

steps.title: Manage version upgrades and change
steps.description: Set up a repeatable upgrade process: load the new version into a test environment, identify additions, changes, and inactivations, use history data to find replacements for inactive content used in templates, value sets, and queries, run regression tests with consuming applications, and promote to production with a rollback plan. Notify users before the upgrade goes live. See the Governance playbook for change management.

dependencies.text: SNOMED CT license and access to release packages (via MLDS or your NRC)
The editions, versions, and language reference sets each consuming system needs
A SNOMED CT-enabled terminology server, or application components that implement the required service types
Technical staff to run the service and terminology staff to manage editions, languages, and upgrades
Access control, audit logging, and availability arrangements for production use

pitfalls: Treating SNOMED CT as a flat code list: services that ignore the hierarchy, reference sets, expression constraints, and history lose most of SNOMED CT's value
Requests that do not identify the edition and version: results change silently when the server is upgraded
Loading only the International Edition when a national edition exists: local concepts, national reference sets, and national language reference sets are missing
No language configuration: services return fully specified names or terms in the wrong language to clinical applications
Applying a single set of delta files after skipping versions: earlier changes are missed
Upgrading without using history data: inactive concepts remain in templates, value sets, and queries with no replacement
Using public servers in production: they are intended for development and evaluation, not clinical use
Caching terms or expansions in applications without a refresh process: cached content diverges from the service after each upgrade

search-ux.title: Search and data entry
search-ux.subtitle: Designing clinician-friendly SNOMED CT search and data entry, using the search capabilities of standard terminology servers
search-ux.overview: Search is where clinicians meet SNOMED CT: almost every coded entry starts with someone typing a few characters and picking from a list. Good search makes the right concept the easiest one to choose; poor search pushes users towards the wrong concept or towards free text. The SNOMED CT Search and Data Entry Guide sets out the core principles: - Scope each field to a clinically appropriate set of active concepts - Match the way clinicians type - word prefixes in any order, with language-appropriate handling of accented characters - Display preferred terms from the user's language reference set, never fully specified names - Order the shortest and most relevant matches first, never alphabetically - Handle no match deliberately, rather than falling back to free text Terminology servers - such as SNOMED International's open source Snowstorm and Snowstorm Lite, and servers and services from other providers - support these principles through the standard FHIR $expand operation. Most of the work is therefore choosing and configuring the server, and designing the user interface around it - not building search from scratch.

decisions.question: What concept scope does each data entry field need?
decisions.guidance: Bind every field to a defined set of concepts, normally an ECL constraint such as << 404684003 |Clinical finding| for a diagnosis field or << 71388002 |Procedure| for a procedure field. Use reference sets where needed to exclude content (for example, the non-human reference set in human medicine). Only active concepts may be selectable: in data entry this is not a user option. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring and testing constraints.

decisions.question: Which terminology server will provide search?
decisions.guidance: Use a terminology server rather than building search yourself: matching, ranking, language handling and release updates are already solved there. Snowstorm suits organisations that need several editions or versions, full ECL and a browser. Snowstorm Lite suits a single edition where fast search, a small footprint or offline use matters. Other providers offer commercial servers and hosted services - see SNOMED International's list of terminology servers and services. Choose a server with a FHIR API, ECL support and text search through FHIR $expand, so the application can stay largely server-independent. A custom database search is only a last resort. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment options.

decisions.question: Which language and dialect will users search in?
decisions.guidance: Configure the server and requests for the language reference set your users work with. Matching should cover preferred terms and acceptable synonyms in that language reference set, and results should display its preferred terms. In search connected to data entry, use one language or dialect only, so that users never see a mix of terms; ordering a user's preferred language first is only for genuinely multilingual settings. See the Multilingual implementation playbook.

decisions.question: How should results be ordered?
decisions.guidance: The guide recommends shortest matching terms first, preferred terms before synonyms, the user's language first in multilingual settings, priority within any active ordered reference set, then frequency of use. Terminology servers provide the base ordering - Snowstorm sorts by length of the matched term, for example - but ordering in FHIR $expand is not standardised, so test it on your server. Frequency boosting usually has to be added by the application. Never sort a broad result set alphabetically: the guide flags this as a patient safety issue.

decisions.question: Should a hand-curated priority subset limit what clinicians can choose?
decisions.guidance: SNOMED International advises against it. A manually enumerated subset caps clinical expressivity, misses new content on each release, and fails rare-disease and specialist use cases. Define the field with ECL and use ordering and frequency to surface common concepts instead. A curated subset is only justified as a temporary workaround in a system that cannot query full SNOMED CT.

steps.title: Define the concept scope for each field
steps.description: Write an ECL constraint for each field, test its expansion with clinical experts, and document it as a named value set that is used both by search and by validation of stored data. Add reference sets where content needs to be excluded or prioritised.

examples.label: ECL constraints for common fields
examples.code:
# Diagnosis or problem field
<< 404684003 |Clinical finding (finding)|

# Disorders only
<< 64572001 |Disease (disorder)|

# Procedure field
<< 71388002 |Procedure (procedure)|

# Allergy causative agent (substances and products)
<< 105590001 |Substance (substance)| OR
<< 373873005 |Pharmaceutical / biologic product (product)|

# Findings without explicit context (exclude 'history of', 'suspected', ...)
<< 404684003 |Clinical finding (finding)| MINUS
<< 413350009 |Finding with explicit context (situation)|

steps.title: Choose and configure the terminology server
steps.description: Load the edition your users need, configure the default language reference set, and check how the server handles accented characters for your language - matching 'sjogren' to 'Sjögren' is right in English but wrong for some Nordic letters. If you use a stop-word list, make sure clinically significant words such as 'no', 'not' and 'without' are never removed. Keep the server on the same release cycle as your edition. Only build search on a custom database if no terminology server can be deployed; the SQL practical guide shows one approach, and you then own matching, ranking and release updates yourself.

options.label: SNOWSTORM
points: Open source, from SNOMED International, built on Elasticsearch
Full ECL 2.0; multiple editions, extensions and versions on one server
Word-prefix, any-order matching sorted by length of the matched term, with configurable language-specific character folding
FHIR API plus a native API that can return the matched description and search by semantic tag
Needs more infrastructure; suited to shared or national services

options.label: SNOWSTORM LITE
points: Open source, from SNOMED International, built for fast search with a small memory footprint (around 500 MB once indexed)
One edition per server; FHIR API only; supports ECL Core, a subset of ECL
Most relevant results first, multiple languages with configurable character folding
Suited to responsive data entry, autoscaling, offline and low-connectivity settings; not intended as a national terminology server

options.label: OTHER SERVERS AND SERVICES
points: Commercial servers and hosted services are available from several providers - see the list of terminology servers and services
Check FHIR $expand text filtering, the ECL version supported, language and character handling, and ranking of results
Check how many editions and versions can be hosted, how new releases are loaded, and the licensing and hosting terms

steps.title: Implement search through the terminology server
steps.description: For type-ahead search, call FHIR ValueSet/$expand with the field's value set (or an ECL-based implicit value set), the text the user has typed as the filter, a small count, and the display language. This works the same way on any FHIR terminology server. Wait for two or three characters and a short pause in typing before calling, and always request active concepts only. Each concept appears once in an expansion, displayed with its preferred term, which avoids multiple hits on the same concept. The expansion does not say which synonym matched; if you need to show it (for example 'Heart attack' beside 'Myocardial infarction'), use the server's native search API where available.

examples.label: FHIR $expand type-ahead search
examples.code:
# User has typed "heart att" in a diagnosis field
GET [base]/ValueSet/$expand
  ?url=http://snomed.info/sct?fhir_vs=ecl/<< 404684003
  &filter=heart att
  &count=10
  &activeOnly=true
  &displayLanguage=en

# URL-encode the parameter values in a real request.
# Response (abbreviated): one entry per concept, preferred term as display
"expansion": {
  "contains": [
    { "system": "http://snomed.info/sct",
      "code": "22298006",
      "display": "Myocardial infarction" }
  ]
}

steps.title: Order and display the results
steps.description: Show preferred terms, never fully specified names, and check the server's ordering against the guide's principles with real clinical searches. Add frequency boosting in the application if needed, tracking selections per field, service or role and seeding the data at go-live from existing coded data. Where two different concepts share the same term, show enough context to tell them apart - for example the parent concept or semantic tag on hover. For very large result sets, consider grouping results under their parent concepts. Mnemonics and personal favourites can speed up entry of frequent concepts, but only alongside search that is easy to use; otherwise users pick the nearest shortcut even when it is the wrong concept.

steps.title: Design the no-match pathway
steps.description: When nothing suitable is found, say so clearly and offer a route forward: suggestions for alternative or broader terms, and a way to request new content from your terminology team or SNOMED International. Never allow silent free-text entry in a field meant for SNOMED CT codes. If a field often ends in no match, review its scope, language configuration and synonyms before considering anything else.

steps.title: Test with clinicians and iterate
steps.description: Test with clinicians from the target specialties using realistic scenarios before go-live, and keep measuring afterwards: time to selection, how often the intended concept is in the first few results, and how often users reach the no-match pathway. Include specific checks for accented characters, negation words, abbreviations and common misspellings. Use the findings to tune scope, language configuration and ordering.

dependencies.text: Terminology server with FHIR $expand text filtering and ECL - for example Snowstorm, Snowstorm Lite, or a server or service from another provider
ECL-defined value set for every data entry field
Language reference set configured for matching and preferred term display
Clinical users from the target specialties available for usability testing

pitfalls: Displaying fully specified names in search results - they are for disambiguation, not for clinical display
Searching all of SNOMED CT without a field scope - users get irrelevant results and pick the wrong concepts
Sorting broad result sets alphabetically - the best match disappears down the list, a documented patient safety issue
Allowing silent free text when nothing matches - structured data quality is lost without anyone noticing
Using a generic stop-word list - words such as 'no', 'not' and 'without' change clinical meaning and must stay searchable
Building search on a custom database or static export without a release process - new concepts never appear and inactive ones stay selectable
Letting favourites or mnemonics replace search - users choose the nearest shortcut even when it is the wrong concept

mapping.title: Mapping SNOMED CT to/from other code systems
mapping.subtitle: Mapping SNOMED CT to and from classification, billing, and other code systems, for reporting, interoperability, or analysis
mapping.overview: Maps connect SNOMED CT with other code systems so that data recorded once can be reused for other purposes. Each map works in one direction: some take SNOMED CT data out to classifications such as ICD-10, others bring data coded in local, legacy or other code systems into SNOMED CT. Used well, maps are essential: - Reuse without re-coding - SNOMED CT-coded records can feed statistical returns, registries and funding with less manual coding - Bridging systems - systems using different code systems can exchange and compare data while they move to a common terminology - Unlocking existing data - legacy and external data can be analysed alongside native SNOMED CT data But a map is not always the right answer: - Meaning shifts wherever source and target are not equivalent, and a map cannot simply be reversed - Maintenance never ends - the map must be updated whenever the source, the target, or the use case changes - Existing maps, such as SNOMED International's SNOMED CT to ICD-10 map, are almost always better than building a new one This playbook covers deciding whether to map, building or adopting a map, applying it correctly, and keeping it current. Moving a system of record onto SNOMED CT is covered in the Migrating to SNOMED CT playbook.

decisions.question: Is a map the right solution?
decisions.guidance: Before building a map, ask whether the requirement can be met another way, and whether the cost of maintaining the map is justified. If the goal is SNOMED CT-coded data, capturing SNOMED CT directly at the point of documentation is usually more accurate long-term. If the goal is ICD-10 or another classification, trained clinical coders working from the SNOMED CT record may produce more accurate, comparable data than a map. Where a map is part of retiring a legacy system, see the Migrating to SNOMED CT playbook.

decisions.question: What is the map for, and what does that require of it?
decisions.guidance: The use case determines the map's direction, the patterns it allows, and how close each match must be. A map is unidirectional unless every link is an exact equivalent. Funding and statistical grouping need each source code in exactly one category (one-to-one or many-to-one) and usually accept broader targets; data integration and decision support need equivalence. Agree the allowed patterns and relationship types (equivalent, broader, narrower, inexact, no match) before mapping starts, and document them as mapping rules.

decisions.question: Does a suitable map already exist?
decisions.guidance: Check whether SNOMED International, your national release centre, or another organisation already maintains a map for this purpose - for example, the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 map, distributed with the International Edition. An actively maintained existing map is almost always preferable to a custom one, which needs its own upkeep on every release of both code systems.

decisions.question: How will the map be represented and distributed?
decisions.guidance:
Choose the representation by who will use the map and how it must be maintained, not by the tool that produced it:
  • Map reference set in an extension - when the map is shared beyond one system (for example a national or organisation-wide map, or a map supporting a messaging specification) and must be versioned and released with SNOMED CT. It is uniquely identified, carries the same versioning and module dependencies as SNOMED CT components, is distributed with the edition, and can still be served as a FHIR ConceptMap by a terminology server. It requires an extension namespace and release process - see the Extensions playbook.
  • FHIR ConceptMap - when the map supports a specific integration, project or FHIR-based exchange and does not need to be released with SNOMED CT. Give it a canonical URL and version, and record the SNOMED CT edition and version it was built against.
  • Proprietary or internal structure - only for a map used inside a single system and never shared. It is hard to share, audit and maintain, so it still needs documented source and target versions and a change history.
Whichever form is chosen, the map must be uniquely identified, versioned, and documented.

decisions.question: How will source codes with no suitable target be handled?
decisions.guidance: Some source codes have no adequate target. Agree the options in advance: request new content from the code system owner, add a concept in an extension, use a postcoordinated expression (only if every system downstream can consume it), or record the code as having no target. Do not force an approximate match to improve coverage figures.

decisions.question: What level of review does the clinical risk require?
decisions.guidance: Match the review approach to the risk and the resources available. A single author with no reviewer is only suitable for small, low-risk maps not used clinically. Single author with a reviewer is common; dual independent authoring with an adjudicator is the gold standard where errors could affect care. Treat automated and AI-assisted suggestions as one more mapper, not as reviewed output. Document the risk assessment and the chosen approach as part of the map documentation.

steps.title: Define the purpose, scope and mapping rules
steps.description: Document what the map is for, who will use it, and the source and target scope. When mapping into SNOMED CT, constrain the target to the relevant hierarchy, subhierarchy or subset - for example, Clinical finding for conditions, Body structure for body sites - which improves both automated suggestions and human consistency. Record the mapping rules from the decisions above (direction, allowed patterns, relationship types, how to handle no-match codes) and editorial guidelines for recurring cases, and keep them up to date as the work progresses.

examples.label: Mapping rules by use case
examples.code:
Use case                                   Patterns       Relationship types
------------------------------------------ -------------- ------------------------------
SNOMED CT to classification for funding    1:1, N:1       Broader allowed
Legacy code set in a clinical system to    1:1, 1:N, N:1  Equivalent, narrower, broader
  SNOMED CT (migration)
Partner system codes to SNOMED CT for      1:1, N:1       Equivalent only
  decision support

# Also record: map direction (unidirectional), target scope
# (e.g. << 404684003 |Clinical finding|), no-match policy,
# and whether postcoordinated targets are allowed

steps.title: Prepare the source data
steps.description: A map cannot fix poor-quality source data. Review source codes and terms for ambiguous abbreviations, symbols and free-text artefacts, agree interpretation rules for them, and flag entries that need clinical input rather than forcing a guess. Group similar terms (all fractures, all diabetes terms) and identify duplicates to make mapping faster and more consistent. Where usage data is available, consider whether codes that have never been used need mapping at all.

steps.title: Adopt or build the map
steps.description: Choose the path that matches the decisions above. Whichever path is taken, publish the map in the form chosen above - a map reference set in an extension, or a FHIR ConceptMap - so that terminology services and downstream systems can use it the same way. Building a map of any size needs dedicated mapping tooling: working in spreadsheets is slow and error-prone, and gives no review workflow or audit trail. SNOMED International provides Snap2SNOMED, a freely available tool for mapping to SNOMED CT, and commercial mapping tools are also available - see the list of mapping tools.

options.label: ADOPT AN EXISTING MAP
points: Load the map into your terminology service from the release files - the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 map is an extended map reference set (447562003)
Check that its scope, target version and documented assumptions fit your use case

Use the map with the SNOMED CT release it was published for where possible; if your release differs, identify concepts that are new, inactivated or changed since then and resolve them - new concepts will have no map rows, and inactivated ones can be traced through historical associations
Rule-based maps must be applied with their full algorithm - see step 4

options.label: MAP OUT OF SNOMED CT
points: Author each source concept's target and relationship type within the agreed rules
Use a simple map reference set where targets are one-to-one; a complex or extended map reference set where a concept needs several targets or a choice between them
Where the choice depends on patient context (age, sex, other conditions), express it as map rules with readable advice

options.label: MAP INTO SNOMED CT
points: Search within the agreed target scope, and confirm each candidate's meaning from its fully specified name and defining relationships, not its preferred term alone
Where the rules allow, choose the most general concept that fully matches the source meaning
Use a mapping tool such as Snap2SNOMED (free from SNOMED International): automated suggestions, author and reviewer roles, audit trail, and export as a FHIR ConceptMap
For codes with no suitable concept, follow the agreed no-match policy

steps.title: Apply rule-based maps correctly
steps.description: Maps such as the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 map are not a lookup table. Each source concept can have several map groups, each producing at most one target code. Within a group, rules are evaluated in priority order and the first rule that is true selects the target; rules can test the patient's age, sex or other recorded conditions, and advice explains each choice to a human. Some concepts cannot be classified without information the record does not hold. The map supports semi-automated coding: it is not designed to fully automate ICD-10 coding, so plan for coder review of the output. Systems that cannot evaluate the rules can present the map advice to the user instead. To see how map groups, rules and advice work in practice, try the SNOMED Maps Demonstrator, which applies the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 and ICD-11 maps including their complex rules.

examples.label: Extended map rows for one concept
examples.code:
# 447562003 |SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map|
# Source: 15296000 |Sterility (finding)|

Group Priority Rule                                     Target
1     1        IFA 10114008 |Female sterility (finding)|  N97.9
1     2        IFA 49408009 |Male sterility (finding)|    N46
1     3        OTHERWISE TRUE                            (none)
               advice: MAP SOURCE CONCEPT CANNOT BE
                       CLASSIFIED WITH AVAILABLE DATA

# A simple lookup returns all three rows. Correct application
# evaluates the rules against the patient record and selects
# one row per group.

examples.label: Map application algorithm

steps.title: Review and test the map
steps.description: Review the map at three levels: design (does the map meet its requirements?), content (are the targets right for each source code?), and use (does it work in the system and workflow where it will be applied?). Use the review approach agreed for the map's risk, and check automated or AI-suggested targets with particular care - identifiers that do not match their descriptions, or plausible but imprecise targets, are common. Keep AI-suggested and human-approved maps clearly distinguished. Test end to end with realistic data, including unmapped, multi-target and rule-dependent codes, and confirm that output for statutory or contractual reporting meets its requirements.

steps.title: Maintain the map with each release
steps.description: Review the map whenever the source code system, the target code system, or the use case changes. New source codes need new rows; retired source codes need their rows removed - when SNOMED CT is the source, use historical associations to find the replacement concepts; retired target codes need a new target; and non-equivalent maps should be re-evaluated in case a better target now exists. Version every map release, keep a change log, and tell the systems and teams that use the map what is changing before it goes live. See the Governance playbook for release management.

dependencies.text: Terminology service that can load map reference sets and serve them as FHIR ConceptMaps ($translate) - see the Terminology service playbook
Existing maps for your target, where available, such as the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 map from the International Edition release files
Mapping tool with review workflow and audit trail - Snap2SNOMED (free, for mapping to SNOMED CT) or a commercial tool
Mappers and reviewers with clinical knowledge and expertise in both code systems
Map documentation covering purpose, scope, mapping rules, risk assessment and review approach
Governance process for change requests, versioning and release of the map

pitfalls: Treating a rule-based map as a simple lookup - every candidate target is returned, and the wrong code is selected or several codes are reported
Using a map in the reverse direction - non-equivalent links add or lose meaning, and reversing a SNOMED CT to classification map can imply clinical detail that was never recorded
Building a custom map when a maintained one already exists - the custom map then needs its own upkeep on every release
Mapping into SNOMED CT without constraining the target scope - automated and human mappers both pick plausible concepts from the wrong hierarchy
Accepting automated or AI-suggested targets without review - suggested identifiers may not exist or may not match their descriptions
Expecting mapped data to match native SNOMED CT data - a map reproduces the source's granularity, so reports built on mapped data may not be comparable
No maintenance process, or changes made without notice - the map drifts out of date, and downstream reports, billing and coding shift without anyone knowing why
